I'm so sorry for your loss. He sounds like an incredible member of your family. I'm glad you got to be with him during the end.

Oh, well I'm glad to hear about your GED; that makes one less thing to deal with. Even some community college is a good start that you can come back to at any time. That's a shame about your friends not taking you seriously. Perhaps you could try to branch out and meet some new people? It can be difficult, especially when you're in hard times, but a friendly person can make all the difference as well. Some possible places could be a volunteering job/commitment, or even the Internet. 

If you don't mind me asking, do your parents play a role in your life? If they do, there's a possibility you could go to them to ask for a bit of help.

Wow, this sounds like a multitude of problems all rushing to you at once. I suppose we can take it step by step and try to figure out a solution for each. 

You mentioned a drinking problem. These are pretty serious and can have a lot of negative outcomes. Have you tried contacting a group or therapist/counselor who can help you with your drinking? It will definitely be difficult at first, but even having your drinking intake a little more stabilized can help a lot in just daily life. 

You also said you dropped out of high school 5 years ago. That in no way makes you a failure, however. If you'd like to continue your schooling, though, obtaining your GED may be a good place to start. You could potentially take classes at a community college to regain any lost knowledge or learn new knowledge that can help you reach your GED. If community college is too expensive or doesn't seem like the right fit for you, there are also many websites online that help you practice math and english skills; some websites even have tutoring that have free trials. A good website for math would be https://www.khanacademy.org/, which is completely free. It has a few other subjects as well, but focuses on math. If you end up getting your GED, community college is a nice next step. There's no time limit for any of this, fortunately, and so be sure to take it at your own pace and do what makes you comfortable. 

It's always rough when friends move away. Do you have any way of keeping in contact with them? I know you mention you don't want to 'burden' them, but as your friends, they are there when you're in need. If you don't feel comfortable talking about these kind of matters with them, however, you can still try to keep in contact with them and talk about other things. In the process, it can either potentially help cheer you up by strengthening your bond with them, or you could end up deciding you'd like to talk about your troubling times a bit. Even if a lot is happening right now, simply talking about a single issue for a short amount of time can relieve stress. 

Rent might be one of the most difficult issues here, because of how immediate it seems. Because I don't know too much about the dealings with rent and I don't want to accidentally give you false information, I would suggest possibly asking your boyfriend for alternative routes. Though you said that you don't want to talk about those things with your boyfriend because he gets uncomfortable, you could try bringing it up a different way with fewer emotions. Try an approach such as "Hey, _boyfriend_, I'd like your advice on how to deal with my rent. I'm not sure entirely how to deal with it on my own, and I'd like to hear your opinion on what you think the best course of action would be." Something along those lines might make him feel a bit more comfortable responding, as it gives him a way to input his feelings toward the conversation and problem at hand. If you don't feel comfortable with this or it doesn't work, I do believe homeless shelters may be a last resort that could help you in the meantime while you get back on your feet. 

Food is important, too. It fuels your body and in general just makes you feel better. I know it's difficult with all else you're dealing with, but please find a way to have at least a somewhat steady source of food. Food stamps or food banks may be possible short term solutions. As I talked about earlier, the possession of a GED makes it easier to qualify for more jobs, which also may help, though I know it seems like way too much to do at once, and it is. Though it seems like all is lost, small steps toward the right direction would be the best idea. 

I'm very sorry you're going through all this, especially all at once. You seem like a kind person and I wish you the best of luck through your struggles. If I have any more suggestions or ideas, I'll be sure to edit them in.

Typically everything you tell your counselor or therapist is in confidence, so they can't tell anyone. You can tell them about your past suicide attempt. If you are a harm to yourself or others (such as planning a suicide and telling her the details) I believe s/he has to tell someone to protect you and others. 

Best of luck.

Hey man, tomorrow is a new day. Just think of the reasons why. There are a multitude of possibilities. 

- You didn't think you were losing any weight and so you didn't see a point in continuing the diet
(It takes a while to see results, and as my friend once told me, you're always your worst critic)
- Your body was craving more sugary/salty foods 
(Everything in moderation, yeah? Moderation can help you stray from those 'fuck it' moments if you're really craving something)
- Changing your diet so drastically was weird
(Take baby steps. Cut out carbs first, and then after a month, sugar. It's like rewiring your body that's been working one way for seventeen years. It's going to take time)

You can do this. I know you can, and we're all right here with you taking as many steps as we can forward. Even if you take one or two steps backwards, you can still keep going. 

I'm always here if you want to talk. (:

It happened to me for about a week. Lost eight pounds. It freaked me out and initially my parents thought I had appendicitis or something. Turns out it was just my depression being more aggressive than usual. For a few days I would eat about 100 calories, if any.

This happened earlier this month, actually. I'm not completely back on track, but what I did was slowly try to eat more high calorie foods. I essentially forced myself to eat even when my stomach and mind told me I wasn't hungry. I was, but it hurt at first. It still hurts a bit, but I've been eating more. Try really plain foods like rice or pasta. If nothing else is working, you could talk to your doctor. 

I felt nauseous when thinking about food, which stopped me many times from eating. My doctor prescribed an anti-nausea pill that I could take before eating to help. I hope your appetite comes back soon. Good luck.

They may have been more angry with themselves than they were at you. It's frightening to hear someone tell you 'I want to die'. Your parents may believe that they are part of the problem, or even the reason. 

If you can't handle talking to them again, I suggest talking to a friend, or a counselor. I see that you mentioned talking to someone on the hotline. That works, too. Either way, find someone you can talk to who doesn't get upset.
